home.t01: The letter with no return address
home.t02: The Hunt for the Hidden Word
home.t03: The Archivist's map. Nine numbered places, no route.
home.t04: Somewhere between the Santa Susana Mountains and the Simi Hills, a valley is keeping a secret it has kept for a very long time.
home.t05: The story begins with a letter. It arrives with no return address — only a hand-drawn map of nine places in Simi Valley and one line of instruction: Nine objects. Nine letters. One word. Go in any order you like.
home.t06: The letter is signed by a woman who called herself the Valley Archivist. For forty years she collected the things this valley almost forgot: a coin from a famous speech, a strip of film from a western that was never released, a lantern from a ranch kitchen, a whistle from the last freight train, a basket woven the old way, a key cut from sandstone, a bell from the hilltop cross, a mask from an empty stage, and a seed medallion from the park where the valley comes to rest on Sunday afternoons.
home.t07: Before she disappeared, she hid all nine. Not to lose them — to make someone look.
home.t08: Here is what she understood. You cannot simply carry these objects out of the valley. Each one is guarded by a piece of language. To take an object, you have to earn it: you have to think in English quickly and confidently, the way you will need to think when you stand in front of a room and pitch your idea.
home.t09: So the hunt is also a training ground. At every location you learn one piece of a system built for adults who need results, not grammar lectures. Then you play for the object until the language stops feeling foreign.
home.t10: There is no correct route, and the Archivist was clear about that. Start at the library on the hill, or the ranch in the rocks, or the old depot by the tracks — it makes no difference. Some hunters begin with the puzzle that looks easiest. Some begin with the place they can already picture. The valley keeps no score on the order.
home.t11: Every object you win carries a letter, and the letters mean nothing on their own. Collect all nine and they arrange themselves, and the word they spell is the name of the place that has been under your feet the entire time.
home.t12: Nine locations. Nine objects. Any order. Open the map and choose your first.
home.mapAlt: Illustrated map of Simi Valley, California, with the nine numbered hunt locations

final.t03: You walked the valley in your own order, and every object came out of its hiding place the same way: you earned it in English. Watch the letters arrive.
final.t05: The word was under your feet the whole time.
final.t08: Nine ideas, and every one of them portable: movement before rules, two kinds of verb, one sentence frame, the six forms of V1, the three helpers of V2, five ways to ask, five small rules that clean up your English, two American sounds, and a method for turning words you recognise into words you use.
final.t09: That is the whole system. The next room you present in is the real final challenge.
final.t11: Playing again clears your collection and sends all nine objects back into hiding.

credits.t02: Who and what made this hunt
credits.t04: The nine concepts come from the Alternative Grammar system — the author's own V1 / V2 / SVN teaching material, written for adults who need working English rather than grammar labels. The theory panels rewrite that material for a business and marketing audience; the structure, the vocabulary of the method and the mnemonics behind it belong to the author.
credits.t06: All nine locations are real places in Simi Valley, California: the Ronald Reagan Presidential Library, Corriganville Park, Strathearn Historical Park, the Santa Susana Depot, the Chumash Indian Museum, Rocky Peak Park, the Mount McCoy cross, the Simi Valley Cultural Arts Center and Rancho Simi Community Park.
credits.t07: The nine objects, the Valley Archivist and the hunt itself are fiction, written for this game and inspired by the history, landscape and film heritage of the valley.
credits.t09: Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript. No frameworks, no build step, no external assets. Progress lives in your browser's local storage under a single key, so the hunt remembers you between sessions and forgets you the moment you press Reset Hunt.
credits.t10: Pronunciation rounds use the browser's own speech features when they are available, and fall back to a listening round when they are not.
credits.t11: Nine locations. Nine objects. Any order.

place01.t03: Hidden here: Silver Speech Coin 🪙 — clear ten rounds and it is yours.
place01.t04: Why you already know more English than you can speak
place01.t05: You have read hundreds of English words this month. You have understood emails, dashboards, product docs, LinkedIn posts. And still, in a meeting, the sentence arrives late — or never. That gap is not a knowledge problem. It is a retrieval problem.
place01.t06: This method fixes retrieval by attaching every new word to a movement or an image before you try to store it as a rule. It is called TPR — Total Physical Response — and it is the reason a child learns "jump" in one afternoon and an adult learns it in three weeks.
place01.t07: Two sides of learning: the left side stores words, the right side produces them
place01.t09: See the word → attach a movement or picture → recall it fast, out loud. Repeat until the recall is faster than the translation. A word that survives that loop behaves like a native word: it shows up when you need it.
place01.t10: What this changes in a business meeting
place01.t11: You stop translating. Translation costs two seconds, and two seconds is the difference between leading a discussion and following it.
place01.t12: You practise production, not recognition. Recognising "forecast" on a slide is free. Saying "our forecast slipped" is the skill worth training.
place01.t13: You use fewer rules. Nine ideas cover almost everything in this system. The rest is repetition with movement.
place01.t15: The Archivist's coin was struck for a speech given on this hill. To lift it, connect each business action to the picture it makes in the room — the same pairing your memory needs.
place01.svg03: Sees the word and files it away

place02.t03: Hidden here: Ironwood Film Reel 🎞️ — clear ten rounds and it is yours.
place02.t04: Every English verb is one of two characters
place02.t05: Corriganville was a film ranch. Westerns were shot in these rocks, and every western needs two characters: the boss who never explains himself, and the old man who cannot cross the street without a cane. English verbs cast the same two roles.
place02.t07: am · is · are · was · were · will be
place02.t08: Strong. Asks its own questions — no help required. Only allows a noun, a feeling or a situation next to it.
place02.t10: V2 The one with the cane
place02.t12: Weak. Cannot ask a question alone. It borrows a helper: Do, Does, Did, Will.
place02.t13: We launched the campaign. → Did we launch the campaign?
place02.t14: The hand test — two seconds, always works
place02.t15: Can you do it with your hands or your body? Then it is V2 (send, present, negotiate, build). Can't you? Then you are looking at V1 — the verb "to be" and nothing else.
place02.t25: Does the team ship on Friday?
place02.t32: Why this one idea carries the rest
place02.t33: Once you can name the character, you already know how to ask, how to answer and where to put "not". Locations 4 and 5 give you the exact forms. This location trains the split until it is instant.

place03.t03: Hidden here: Miner's Brass Lantern 🏮 — clear ten rounds and it is yours.
place03.t04: One shape covers almost every answer you will give
place03.t05: The oldest house in this park was built from a plan so simple the family could raise the frame themselves. English answers work the same way. There is one frame, and roughly nineteen out of twenty sentences sit on it.
place03.t07: Subject — who or what. Verb — V1 or V2. Noun — the thing, the feeling or the situation. Then stop. The full stop is part of the rule: adults lose sentences by continuing past the noun.
place03.t08: The three blocks of a sentence: subject, verb, noun
place03.t09: The frame at work in a real meeting
place03.t26: Spanish lets you drop the subject. English does not. "Is ready" is not a sentence; "The demo is ready" is. When a sentence collapses mid-air, the missing block is almost always the subject.
place03.t28: Before you speak, decide the three blocks in order: who, which verb, what thing. Say them. Stop. Anything extra — time, place, detail — you can add afterwards as a second short sentence.

place04.t03: Hidden here: Iron Rail Whistle 🚂 — clear ten rounds and it is yours.
place04.t04: Six words, three times, no exceptions
place04.t05: A depot runs on a timetable, and V1 is the timetable of English. It has six forms in total. Learn the grid below and the entire "to be" family is finished — present, past and future.
place04.t06: V1 forms and how to flip them into questions
place04.t12: Am I…? Are you…? Is he…?
place04.t19: The question is a swap, not a new sentence
place04.t20: Take the statement and move V1 to the front. The report is ready → Is the report ready? Nothing else moves. This is why V1 needs no helper: it is strong enough to lead.
place04.t22: Yes: S + V1 + N. — Yes, they were in the call.
place04.t23: No: S + V1 + not + N. — No, they weren't in the call.
place04.t24: "Not" always sits immediately after V1. Never before it, never at the end.
place04.t25: When an action verb stands next to V1
place04.t26: A V2 cannot act next to the boss, so it changes costume and becomes a situation: add -ing or -ed. We are presenting on Thursday. The proposal was approved. In both cases the word after V1 behaves like a noun, exactly as the frame requires.
place04.t27: Meeting phrases built on V1 alone
place04.t28: I am ready. The numbers are final. That was our best quarter. The client is not convinced. We will be online at nine.

place05.t03: Hidden here: Valley Rain Basket 🧺 — clear ten rounds and it is yours.
place05.t04: Weak verbs, and the three helpers that carry them
place05.t05: Every basket in this valley was built by repeating one weave until the shape held. V2 questions work the same way: one pattern, three helpers, endless sentences.
place05.t07: Choose the helper, keep the verb plain
place05.t14: Did the client approve the budget?
place05.t24: The rule that saves you every time
place05.t25: The helper carries the tense, so the verb stays plain. Did he run — not "did he ran". Does she manage — not "does she manages". The past or the "-s" appears only when the helper disappears.
place05.t26: Answers: the long way and the natural way
place05.t27: Did he present the results? → Long: He did present the results. Natural: He presented the results.
place05.t28: Does he report to you? → Long: He does report to me. Natural: He reports to me.
place05.t29: Use the long form when you want emphasis — it is how English insists.
place05.t30: Negatives: helper + not, always before the verb
place05.t31: They did not (didn't) send the proposal. We do not (don't) discount below ten percent. She will not (won't) join the call.

place06.t03: Hidden here: Amber Sandstone Key 🗝️ — clear ten rounds and it is yours.
place06.t04: Five words that decide how you sound in a room
place06.t05: The trail up Rocky Peak has five gates, and each one asks a different question: may I pass, should I pass, must I pass. English has the same five, and choosing the wrong one is how a polite request lands as a demand.
place06.t15: Could you send me the deck?
place06.t18: May I add one point before we close?
place06.t20: Asking for or giving an opinion
place06.t24: We must deliver before the launch.
place06.t26: They behave exactly like Did / Do / Will
place06.t27: They go to the front, and the verb after them stays plain. Can she join? — not "can she joins". Negatives keep the same position: We should not discount this deal.
place06.t29: Should asks for an opinion. Must states a requirement. Say "you must send the invoice today" to a client and you have given an order; say "you should send the invoice today" and you have given advice. In English the difference is the whole sentence.
place06.t31: Asking a favour upwards? Could. Asking a colleague? Can. Speaking to a room of executives? May. Recommending? Should. Stating a deadline? Must.

place07.t03: Hidden here: Hilltop Bell 🔔 — clear ten rounds and it is yours.
place07.t04: Five small rules that clean up your English
place07.t05: From the cross on this hill you can see the whole valley at once. Same idea here: five short rules, each fixing a mistake that professionals repeat for years.
place07.t06: 1 · Place and time: under, on, at, in
place07.t16: The figures are on the slide. We ship on Monday.
place07.t18: Inside something, or a month or year
place07.t19: The data is in the report. We launch in March.
place07.t23: 2 · Adjectives describe nouns, adverbs describe actions
place07.t24: An adjective sits next to a thing. An adverb — usually ending in -ly — sits next to a V2. The angry client (adjective) answered angrily (adverb). In business writing: a quick decision vs we decided quickly.
place07.t26: Let's is short for "let us", and it is the fastest way to move a room. Formula: Let's + V2 (+ noun) — Let's start. Let's review the numbers. Let's take this offline.
place07.t28: Since = one starting point: since Monday, since 2019, since the merger.
place07.t29: From … to … = two ends of a period: from Monday to Friday, from January to June.
place07.t31: Most of them are near-twins of the word you already use in your first language: information, presentation, negotiation, production. Two things to remember: they are nouns, so they pair with V1 — the presentation is ready — and the ending sounds like "shun", never "tee-on".
place07.t32: Why these five and not fifty
place07.t33: Each one shows up in almost every professional conversation you will have. Fix these and your English stops sounding translated.

place08.t01: Location 8 · Simi Valley Cultural Arts Center
place08.t03: Hidden here: Echo Stage Mask 🎭 — clear ten rounds and it is yours.
place08.t04: Two sounds carry most of the accent
place08.t05: On this stage, actors are trained to find a sound in the body before they find it in the script. American English has two sounds that Spanish speakers rarely make by accident, and both have a physical shortcut.
place08.t07: The American R — a low growl, tongue pulled back, jaw loose. It never taps like the Spanish r.
place08.t08: Practise on: person, work, first, return, quarter.
place08.t10: The long E — a wide smile, held about three seconds when you drill it. In a southern accent it stretches even further.
place08.t11: Practise on: meeting, team, key, agree, stream.
place08.t13: presentation, information, production, negotiation. Say the ending like the English word "shun" and one whole family of vocabulary lands correctly.
place08.t14: Pairs your audience will hear differently
place08.t31: Your browser may offer a microphone check. If it does not, or you would rather not speak out loud right now, the game switches to a listening round — you hear the word and choose the sound family. Both paths count.

place09.t03: Hidden here: Yucca Seed Medallion 🌿 — clear ten rounds and it is yours.
place09.t04: A full refrigerator is not a meal
place09.t05: You have thousands of English words in storage. You recognise them instantly when you read them. And yet, at 10:04 on a Tuesday, in front of a client, the shelf looks empty.
place09.t06: That is the difference between passive vocabulary — words you recognise — and active vocabulary — words that arrive when you open your mouth. Learners spend years adding ingredients to the fridge and almost no time cooking.
place09.t08: A word is active when you can produce it in your own sentence, at speed, without translating. Anything else is still an ingredient.
place09.t09: The personal dictionary — four steps per word
place09.t10: Capture it. Every new word you hear or read that day goes into one place. One notebook, one file, one note app.
place09.t11: Label it. Is it a noun, a V1, a V2, an adjective? This is what tells you where it can sit in a sentence.
place09.t12: Own it. Write two or three sentences of your own — about your work, your product, your week. Not the dictionary's sentence. Yours.
place09.t13: Pair it. Learn the words that travel with it. English is full of fixed pairs: launch a campaign, close a deal, hit a target, raise a concern. Collocation tools such as OZDIC and the Cambridge dictionary's audio are built for this.
place09.t14: Same word, from ingredient to meal
place09.t21: Our forecast is conservative this quarter.
place09.t25: We onboard new clients in two weeks.
place09.t26: onboard a client, a team, a tool
place09.t29: The client raised one concern about pricing.
place09.t31: Ten words a week beats a hundred
place09.t32: Ten words taken all the way to active — labelled, used in your own sentences, paired with their partners — will change how you sound in a meeting. A hundred recognised words will not.

note.1: Did carries the past, so approve goes back to its plain form.
note.2: Does takes the -s away from manage.

note.8: Without Does, third person singular gets its -s back.
note.9: We takes Do, and hire stays plain.

note.1: May is the formal permission word — right for a board room.
note.2: Could softens the request without making it formal.
note.3: Must states an obligation with no room to negotiate.
note.4: Should asks for an opinion, not for permission.
note.5: Can is the everyday permission word between colleagues.
note.6: Can asks about possibility, and the verb after it stays plain.
note.7: Should is advice. Must would sound like an order.
note.8: Could is the safest register with a client.
note.9: A rule that cannot be broken takes must.
note.10: May keeps a written request formal and polite.
note.11: The helper carries the tense, so the verb stays plain.
note.12: Not sits straight after the helper: should not discount.

game06.instructions: Choose the helper that matches the situation. Register matters as much as grammar. Ten correct answers win the key.

detail.1: At marks an exact point in time.
detail.2: In wraps around months, years and seasons.
detail.3: On sits with surfaces — and with days: on Monday.
detail.4: Under means below the line you set.
detail.5: An adverb describes an action verb; adjectives describe nouns.
detail.6: Decision is a noun, so it takes an adjective.
detail.7: Let's + V2 is the fastest way to move a meeting.
detail.9: From … to … marks both ends of a period.
detail.10: Nouns in -tion pair with V1: the presentation is ready.
detail.12: Days of the week take on.
detail.14: The -ly form describes how the action happened.
